This question can't be answered reliably within the ligand-field model, so I'm not giving numbers for Dq, B or C.

**Why Dq is not determined.** [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]²⁺ is d⁹ and Jahn–Teller distorted, so it is tetragonal (D4h), not octahedral. The hole sits in the d(x²−y²) orbital. The three spin-allowed d–d transitions go from the ²B1g ground state to ²A1g (dz²), ²B2g (dxy) and ²Eg (dxz, dyz). In an idealized octahedron, ²Eg → ²T2g would give 10Dq. Here the observed envelope is a single broad, asymmetric band made of overlapping components. The maximum at 14 720 cm⁻¹ and the shoulder at 12 240 cm⁻¹ are not resolved into three transitions. In D4h the one-electron energies depend on the tetragonal splitting parameters Ds and Dt as well as Dq. Two features cannot fix Dq, Ds and Dt together. The band positions also depend on the axial and equatorial ligand-field strengths separately. Taking the maximum as 10Dq, which would give Dq ≈ 1470 cm⁻¹, is only a rough empirical estimate. It is not a real determination.

**Why B is not determined.** B and C are Racah parameters that describe electron–electron repulsion between terms. A d⁹ ion has only one hole, so it has a single ²D free-ion term. That term splits only through the ligand field, and its energies do not depend on B or C. No spin-allowed transition energy depends on B, and no other spin multiplet is available to supply it. The d–d spectrum therefore contains no information about B or C. Any value I gave would be assumed, not derived.

**What can be said.** The band maximum near 14 700 cm⁻¹ is consistent with a strong equatorial field from four NH3 ligands. The shoulder near 12 200 cm⁻¹ is consistent with a lower-energy component such as the dz² transition. The spacing of the components is controlled by the tetragonal distortion. A reliable fit would need the three resolved band energies, for example from Gaussian deconvolution, or polarized single-crystal spectra. Even with those, an angular overlap or D4h model could give the Dq, Ds and Dt combination, but not B.
